title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight: how to spot up to 15 shooting stars an hour in the best display of the year
content:
The Leonid Meteor Shower, one of this year's best-known displays, will peak overnight on 17 November.

One of the more prolific annual meteor showers, it will produce fast, bright meteors that light up the night sky. The shower is active during 6-30 November, but your best view is tonight when around 10 to 15 shooting stars can be seen with the naked eye.

Where to watch the Leonid Meteor Shower

You don't need a telescope or binoculars to see the Leonid Meteor Shower. For the best conditions, find a safe spot away from bright streetlights and light pollution. Wrap up warm, set up a comfy chair, and watch and wait as the stars dazzle above you.

"The meteors can be seen in all parts of the sky, so it's good to be in a wide-open space where you can scan the night sky with your eyes. But if you trace the paths that the meteors take, they seem to originate from the constellation of Leo," say the team at the Royal Museums Greenwich (RMG).

The RMG explains that 2026 is a particularly good year to see the display.

"In 2026, the Leonid meteor shower's maximum occurs on the evening of 17 into the early hours of 18 November, when the Moon will be waxing gibbous. However, the Moon will set just before midnight on this night, allowing you to see the rest of the peak without the Moon's light pollution."

What is the Leonid Meteor Shower?

According to the RMG, the Leonid meteor shower is associated with the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

"The radiant (the point where the meteors seem to stream from) is at the head or 'sickle' of the constellation Leo the Lion, hence the name," the team say.

"As the comet follows its path around the Sun, it leaves a path of tiny debris. The cometary debris enters our planet’s atmosphere at speeds of up to 70 kilometres per second, vaporising and causing the streaks of light we call meteors."

On that note, grab your warm winter coat and head outside tonight to see how many shooting stars you can spot.
